We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is the right one to catch it?"
Asking that question also changed when review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague.
Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. This catches most routine mistakes, and saves team attention for higher-level questions and scrutiny.
— Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang, How the Claude Code team does code review

I’ll start with a nomenclatural sidenote: Apple seems to be going with “Apple HomeView” as the product’s name. E.g., the URL slug for it on Apple.com is apple-homeview/, not just homeview/. Few people notice and no one who doesn’t work in Apple product marketing cares, but they actually do the same thing with Vision Pro — in Cupertino, it’s “Apple Vision Pro” (once again including the URL slug). Yet this week’s new HomePod Mini is just “HomePod mini 2” and the existing 2nd-generation HomePod is just “HomePod (2nd generation)” — not “HomePod 2” or “Apple HomePod”. I certainly intend to just call it “HomeView”.

Apple introduced HomeView with a three-minute introductory film simulating a suburban family’s hectic before-school/work kitchen rush hour, with versions hosted on Apple’s site and YouTube. The most ridiculous aspect of it is that anyone would possibly make their kid French toast in that scenario. I’d have told my son to make his own goddamn French toast with that attitude. Or I’d have made a single serving and eaten it myself right in front of him. Bro.

I do think the basic concept is an intriguing idea. But as an implementation of that concept, my initial impressions are threefold. First, I am unconvinced that anyone in a family would use this for anything other than playing music or podcasts, rather than just using their phones. And if that’s the case, why not just have a HomePod? Apple’s video shows family members taking turns to use the HomeView, rotating it on the kitchen island to face themselves. Why? Why does the mom check her calendar on this, rather than on her iPhone, while the dad is using it to follow a French toast recipe? There’s a real “Why do we need this?” question here and I don’t think Apple’s video answers it, at all. You need to think you want it if you’re going to buy it. And even if you already had a HomeView set up, I’m not sure how often you’d use it instead of your phone, or instead of just talking to it like a screenless HomePod.

Second, all the touching and rotating — in Apple’s own demonstration — makes it seem awkward that HomeView must be tethered to a USB power cable. If you look closely in the video, they do show the USB power cable in some shots, but not many. And if you look really closely, this hypothetical family has drilled a hole in the center of their kitchen island to snake the cable through.
The hero shot introducing the product, of course, does not show the power cable at all:
We see a wee bit of the cable when the dad reaches to touch the screen to start the French toast recipe:

And then a few seconds later, after the mom rotates the HomeView to the side, so she can check her calendar (despite the fact that she knows the dad was using it to follow a recipe), we get our most honest shot of the cabling situation:

The above shot is at 0:49. It’s followed by two quick cuts to the dad and then the younger daughter, then at 0:52 we cut back to the mom (curious about her daughter’s new boyfriend situation), and, lo, the shot is now framed in such a way that we no longer see where the cable goes:

If you think that slight reframing is happenstance, you should stay away from poker tables. Most kitchen islands I’m familiar with — including my own — have power outlets on the sides of the island. I’m sure some people have power outlets on the top surface of the counter, but I can’t recall seeing one. These are kitchen counters, not office desks. But either way, there’d be a long USB-C cable cluttering the countertop. And if you do happen to have a power outlet on the top surface of your counter, there’d be an adapter sticking out of it, all the time, to duplicate this HomeView setup.

This family’s convenient hole in the center of their island countertop is a fantasy. Where does the cable go underneath? How exactly do they have a power adapter plugged in down there? What happens when something spills on the counter? When we custom ordered our kitchen, we weren’t asked if we wanted any holes drilled in our island countertop, and I’d have found it to be a very curious question if I had. It would have made me wonder if the guy asking the question had a hole or two drilled in his head.

I know, it’s a marketing video. Marketing videos present products in ideal settings. But the power cable is an essential aspect of the standalone HomeView. I’m not suggesting that it should be battery powered. You’d still need to plug it in every few days, which would mean most people would just leave it plugged in, which gets us back to needing to live with an always-visible cable and power adapter in one of our living spaces. The countertop hole this cable disappears into in this video is less ideal and more dishonest.

The wall-mounted option seems more appealing to me, but now you’re talking about a home improvement project and (for most of us) calling an electrician. And that raises the question of why the wall-mounted version costs the same $300 as the one with the connected base, even though the base provides the subwoofer. And it requires a mount, and the mounts cost $60 (USB-C), $80 (AC wired), or $130 (PoE — and this one is not available yet). So the wall-mounted version, when you include a mount, costs more but sounds worse? This doesn’t make sense.

Those points make me skeptical that there’s a place for HomeView in my home. We have a stereo pair of HomePods in our kitchen. Neither is on the center island, because that would be dumb. They’re on the counters along the outside of the kitchen, each near an outlet on the wall. In the four days since HomeView was announced, I’ve tried to imagine when I’d want to look at something on a screen on either of them. My count remains at zero.

My third early impression is that the display is surprisingly small. I saw HomeView in person in New York on Tuesday, and I think Apple’s video conveys its size very accurately. It’s small and cute. It’s much more like a HomePod Mini with a screen than a full-size HomePod with a screen. For some reason I was expecting the latter. This size observation is not a complaint, simply an observation. I actually think that making it small and cute makes it about as unobtrusive as an ever-present screen could possibly be. That’s good. But because it’s small you need to be close to it to read anything more detailed than large glanceable widgets.

The major difference between a device with a screen and one without is that you can watch video on a device with a screen. But HomeView clearly isn’t intended for that. It can play video but isn’t primarily meant to play video. If it were it would have a widescreen aspect ratio. But instead it has a square aspect ratio,1 which is decidedly unsuited to video, unless, I suppose, you want a screen that is equally unsuited for both widescreen and tallscreen video.

So my skepticism boils down to the question of why anyone would want to add one (or more!) additional ever-present screens to our homes and lives. Phones can stay in our pockets until we need them. Watches remain on our wrists. HomePods can be tucked away unobtrusively in corners, and remain fully useful. HomeView needs to be in a prominent location for its display to serve any practical purpose. Apple’s initial pitch for it doesn’t earn that prominence for me.

In my thoughts and observations column after Apple’s iPhone event last month, I wrote the following regarding the iPhone Duo’s clever 1:1.4 aspect ratio:


  Here’s the thing. If you take a 2 : 1 or even 2.2 : 1 aspect ratio phone display and turn that into a book-like foldable, the inner screen comes out square — or so close to square that we might as well just call it square. Nobody makes any device of any sort that just has a square display. Square is a terrible aspect ratio for a phone or a tablet or a laptop or a desktop display. The only square displays on the market are the inner displays for Android foldables from the last decade. Square being a shitty aspect ratio is half the reason almost no one has bought those things. 


I will admit that I had the as-yet-unannounced HomeView in mind as I wrote that, given that its square aspect ratio had been rumored for months. HomeView is not a phone or tablet or laptop or desktop display. It’s not a TV either. So maybe square works for this nascent product category (status boards?). But if square does prove to be correct for this purpose, it’ll be the first category I can think of where that’s true. Apple Watch is the closest device I can think of whose screen serves primarily to display status, but even Apple Watch isn’t square. (It varies slightly by model, but Apple Watch displays are around 4 : 5.) ↩︎

blocks.text: October 16, 2026

The App Review Guidelines are a core part of the safe and trusted experience that the App Store strives to offer users around the world — and the foundation of that trust is clear standards that are consistently enforced.

As outlined in our App Review Guidelines, pornographic material has long been prohibited on the App Store — this includes apps that generate nudity or sexually explicit imagery, such as “nudification” apps that create sexually explicit images of real individuals without their consent. Apps that host user-generated content are required to filter objectionable material, give users a way to report offensive content, and let users block abusive accounts. Apps containing hidden or undocumented features are also prohibited on the App Store, including apps that misrepresent their purpose during review and only reveal harmful capabilities — such as “nudification” — after approval, a tactic commonly known as bait-and-switch.

We want great apps and the innovative developers behind them to succeed on the App Store, and as new risks and novel user experiences emerge, we evolve our App Review Guidelines to maintain the trust of users and developers alike. Today we’re publishing updates that strengthen and extend the existing App Store protections, continuing to build on our long-held standards for privacy, quality, and safety.
For complete details, see the App Review Guidelines.
Changes

1.2: Content moderation requirements now explicitly cover nonconsensual intimate imagery — including imagery generated using AI tools — as content that apps must proactively prevent and remove from their platforms. Developers who fail to implement adequate safeguards — or don’t remedy violations after notice — risk violating the Developer Code of Conduct and being removed from the App Store.

2.5.19: This rule clarifies our longstanding prohibition on apps misrepresenting what they do during the App Review process and then changing after approval — for example, adding features or functionality that weren’t included in the version of the app that was submitted to App Review. Apps found engaging in this conduct are subject to removal from the App Store and removal from the Apple Developer Program.

Section 5: The App Store has always prohibited apps that facilitate human trafficking or the exploitation of children (including child sexual abuse material). When we find instances of apps containing such content, we remove them from the App Store. We’ve updated Section 5 of the App Review guidelines to make clear that apps with such content will be removed from the App Store and blocked from alternative distribution.

We’re committed to keeping bad actors off the App Store, with established processes in place to review and act on apps that violate our guidelines. Last year, we prevented over 150K apps with safety issues from reaching customers and terminated over 193K developer accounts for engaging in fraud and abuse. These violations trace back to malicious actors — in some cases coordinated fraud operations — working to conceal harmful content that only becomes active once an app is approved, and as their tactics evolve, we continue to evolve our own tools and resources to prevent and catch this kind of behavior even faster. We do not hesitate to remove apps, and terminate the developers behind them, when they violate these guidelines.

blocks.text: Apple CEO Tim Cook on Monday at the “Spring Forward” media event in San Francisco announced that Apple TV will now cost $69, discounted from its regular price of $99. The new price for the set-top box arrives on the heels of the announcement of HBO Now for Apple TV. The new price appears to apply to the third-generation Apple TV, as the company did not announce a new set-top box on stage at the Yerba Buena Center this afternoon.

A revamped Apple TV has been rumored to be in the works for quite some time, but the next-generation set-top box is not expected to be announced until later this year or beyond. The upcoming Apple TV is expected to have an improved, tactile remote control and a brand new operating system with a built-in App Store. New apps are also expected to have redesigned user interfaces.

blocks.text: The latest version of NetNewsWire for iOS supports iPhone Duo, which is very much a novel iPhone with toolbars running up the side and all kinds of behavior.
How we did it: we didn’t do any work at all. We built the app using Xcode 27.1 and the default iOS SDK that comes with it, and that’s it.

Here’s the thing, though: we were already using standard controls — toolbars, navigation controllers, split views, etc. — and we were paying attention to size classes and such (as opposed to just looking at device type).

There is a good list of reasons to use standard controls in the standard ways, and near the top of that list is to be ready for these kinds of days, so we’re not bogged down for a month or more trying to adapt to big changes like this.
Here’s a secret: Brent didn’t even run this in the Duo simulator before releasing it. We were ready to not claim Duo support and just handle Duo in the next release. But here it is.
PS Of course there may be edge cases and issues in our Duo support we haven’t caught yet. We stand by, as always, ready to field and fix bugs.
PPS Thank you to all the engineers, designers, and testers at Apple who made this work so easily! Again, we didn’t do anything but build with the new SDK. Their achievement is pretty remarkable.

Nine years after first trying to resurrect the Roadster,
Tesla is apparently trying again. CEO Elon Musk might have
relocated its HQ to Texas, but yet again he has returned to
California’s showbiz industry to hawk his wares; last time it was
a Hollywood back lot for the remote-controlled Cybercab
demo, last night it was decades-old stunt

the CEO has a long and glorious history of overpromising and
underdelivering; in 2017 he told attendees at the previous launch
that “We are making it now.” Using the company’s referral program,
some people were in line to receive two free cars. But those free
cars never showed up, and neither did the ones that people put
down $50,000 deposits for; last year Sam Altman discovered how
hard it can be to get that money back.

I like a good stunt show as much as the next guy, and this looked like a cool stunt show. But people are losing their minds if they think this stunt show makes it any more or less likely that Tesla will deliver a Roadster as promised. This Reuters story makes it sound like they think Tesla is going to sell cars that do this stuff. Last night’s stunt show has no more bearing on actual production cars Tesla may or may not ship than George Lucas’s Star Wars movie had on Ronald Reagan’s “Star Wars” missile defense system.

The Tesla Roadster is vaporware. But Elon Musk is very good at distracting from unshipped vaporware by delivering on stunts. Two years ago it was robots that were totally faked. Last night’s car stunt involved real things that actually happened but only in the way that David Copperfield made the Statue of Liberty “disappear”.
Over at Jalopnik, Amber DaSilva has another good take, which concludes:

Tesla has long made up specs for its cars, made wild claims that
weren’t substantiated by users, and now it’s making more big
impressive claims. The “cars” used for the demos were likely
nothing more than shells outfitted with exactly enough equipment
to make the tests work. The 0.81 second zero-to-60 number wasn’t
even shown with an on-screen timer during the event, let alone
independently verified. Tesla has yet to prove anything about the
new Roadster works in the real world, or could even exist within
the realm of physics that those of us not named Musk occupy.

Roadster preorders have reopened, with the company once again
taking $50,000 checks to reserve a car that’ll theoretically be
made two years from now. It hasn’t yet said what will happen to
the people who placed a reservation for the car Tesla announced
nine years ago, which looks and functions completely differently
to the one that bears its name today. And — arguably most
concerning — we don’t know, if Tesla rakes in more money off the
Roadster name, just how much will go to some malicious
end.
And on Threads, Benedict Evans reiterates his longstanding take on what makes Elon Musk so confounding to so many people:

A long time ago, I described Elon Musk as a bullshitter who
delivers. This is the perfect expression of that. This car was
first shown a decade ago, with another stunt, and it never
shipped. Now there’s another stunt, and another huge wave of PR
and admiration.

But meanwhile, there’s the scaled car company, and the
self-landing rockets!

Henry Ford was a brilliant industrialist, a terrible manager and a
racist piece of shit. Several things can be true at once.

If you think Musk is either completely legitimate and trustworthy or an utter fraud, you are wrong. He has led his companies to extraordinary accomplishments, and he has made promises based on complete bullshit. He is a shameless bullshitter who sometimes delivers. The sometimes is implicit in Evans’s take, because if he always delivered, there’d be no bullshit. But I think it’s worth including the sometimes to make the point. And some of the things he’s delivered are so amazing that they sure sounded like they might be bullshit when they were announced. “Space internet” sounded like total bullshit when Musk announced it in 2015, but it started rolling out in 2020, and today you can just buy it at Best Buy for $350.

Tesla makes some tremendous vehicles. Their self-driving technology is the best in the consumer market. (Not as good as Waymo’s, but you can’t buy a Waymo.) So maybe they will ship a great Roadster in 2028. I’ll pay attention if and when they do. But I wouldn’t bet a nickel that they will. And I wouldn’t bet that they won’t, either.

Israeli ad-tech company was a delivery system for "mercenary spyware" (permalink)

More than half of all internet users have installed an ad-blocker; Doc Searls calls it the largest consumer boycott in history. As large as that boycott is, everyone – yes, everyone – should block every "programmatic" ad, because the entire system is so insecure that failing to do so could result in the total compromise of any or all of your digital devices.

That's the inescapable conclusion of Citizen Lab's latest blockbuster investigative report, "Exposing AdFection," which reveals how the largest ad-tech companies in the world, including Google and Facebook, allowed themselves to be hijacked by a "mercenary spyware" company that used the ad system to locate targeted individuals and serve "zero-click malware" that took over their computers and phones without them having to take any action:
https://citizenlab.ca/research/how-discover-tech-turned-targeted-ads-into-a-pipeline-for-spyware/

These tech giants amassed detailed surveillance dossiers on virtually every internet user, and they've assigned each of us unique, persistent identifiers, like a Social Security Number for spying. These companies also allow advertisers – or anyone pretending to be an advertiser – to serve blobs of code (which is all an ad is) to anyone based on those identifiers.

This allowed an Israeli spyware company called Discover-Tech (which masquerades as an ad-tech company) to sell totalitarian governments and sleazy corporate mercenaries the ability to pluck individual internet users out of the billions who log in every day and then serve "malicious ads" (that is, blobs of arbitrary code) to those targeted users. These malicious ads contained "no-click, zero-day" attacks, which meant that they exploited previously unknown vulnerabilities to take over devices without any user interaction. The mere act of loading a web-page or opening an app that relied on one of these gigantic ad-tech companies to serve ads was enough to compromise your device. No clicks needed, and no warning.

Among the targets of this attack campaign were the computers of workers at Al Jazeera. They were attacked with malware from the mercenary spyware company Candiru (which now calls itself "Integrity Labs" because irony is not dead). Beyond Candiru, Discover-Tech also facilitates attacks by numerous criminal mercenary spyware companies, serving ads on hundreds of thousands of sites and apps.

Discover-Tech was "certified" as a safe supplier by Google, Yandex, Microsoft, Beeswax (a division of Comcast) and IAB, the ad-tech industry's leading professional association. Ironically, Discover-Tech even attacked users by serving them malicious GDPR notices that appeared to let users opt out of commercial surveillance.

Because Discover-Tech was certified by all these industry bodies and firms, it had access to more than four billion ad-auctions, meaning that on billions of occasions, it was able to collect the identities of users loading apps and visiting websites, check them against the list of targets, and attack any victims it discovered through this dragnet.

Discover-Tech is an Israeli company with ties to other Israeli spyware and hacking companies, including through its board, whose members included Eric Banoun ("One of the pioneers of offensive cyber in Israel" –Haaretz). They have overlaps, relationships and affiliations with a rogue's gallery of Israeli companies, including the notorious NSO Group, who routinely sell cyber-weapons to the world's worst governments and whose products have been used to attack journalists, embassy workers, and activists.

The whole incident highlights the monumental insecurity of the ad-tech industry, whose indiscriminate and voracious surveillance and manifestly insufficient vetting and security auditing now exposes every internet user in the world to terrifying targeted attacks. These companies – including Google, a thrice-convicted monopolist whose surveillance tendrils are wrapped around the whole world – claim that they operate their networks with prudence and oversight. But the proof is in the pudding: for years, they've played host to a murderer's row of cyber-mercenaries who used their infrastructure to attack journalists and others.

The only way to avoid this is to block ads. This is easy enough to do in a browser (which is why the majority of internet users have installed an ad-blocker in their browsers), but it's illegal to reverse-engineer and modify an app so you can block the ads in it:
https://pluralistic.net/2026/07/21/dickovers/#block-element

Many websites run anti-ad-block scripts that push out nagging, guilt-tripping notices that call you a thief and a cheapskate for blocking ads. Ignore those notices: if a website is running "programmatic" ads that allow arbitrary third parties to spy on billions of people and target individuals for malicious device takeovers, they are charging too high a price to see their content.

Some sites go further: their notices demand that you either turn off your ad-blocker or pay for a subscription. This "pay or okay" scheme is illegal in Europe, California and other territories with strong privacy laws, and they are morally bankrupt besides. Privacy shouldn't be a luxury item and everyone deserves to be secure from cyber-attacks:
https://noyb.eu/en/noybs-pay-or-okay-report-how-companies-make-you-pay-privacy

This report also provides the most comprehensive rebuttal to a dangerous idea that refuses to die: that we should improve competition in the ad-tech sector by assigning every internet user a mandatory, government-issued advertising ID to "democratize" ad-targeting and followup (which the sector calls "attribution"):
https://pluralistic.net/2024/08/07/revealed-preferences/#extinguish-v-improve

Despite all this, none of it is an indictment of ads per se. The problem here isn't advertising, it's surveillance. The ad-tech sector has convinced advertisers that targeting ads to users rather than content will massively improve ad performance. The evidence for this is very poor: targeted ads improve clickthrough rates by less than 5% (relative to content-based ads that relate to the substance of the page you're looking at), and they're incredibly expensive (and very dangerous!) to serve.

On top of all that, surveillance-based ads shift power away from publishers (who know more about the materials they publish than any ad-tech company ever will) to spying ad-tech companies (who can spy on users in ways that no publisher could ever match). Whatever minor additional revenues surveillance advertising can wring out of the market are totally swamped by the cost of the ad-tech sector's own operations, which the ad-tech sector makes up for by grossly underinvesting in security and by colluding to cheat publishers and advertisers, charging more for ads and paying less to the websites that run them:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jedi_Blue

If we want to improve competition in advertising services, the answer isn't to facilitate spying (which also allows the world's scummiest cyber-mercenaries to stage and serve targeted attacks). We should ban surveillance advertising altogether, restoring context-based ads to their role as the way that publishers make an honest living without selling out their audiences:
https://pluralistic.net/2023/05/31/context-ads/#class-formation

That's the inescapable conclusion of Citizen Lab's latest blockbuster investigative report, "Exposing AdFection," which reveals how the largest ad-tech companies in the world, including Google and Facebook, allowed themselves to be hijacked by a "mercenary spyware" company that used the ad system to locate targeted individuals and serve "zero-click malware" that took over their computers and phones without them having to take any action:
https://citizenlab.ca/research/how-discover-tech-turned-targeted-ads-into-a-pipeline-for-spyware/

These tech giants amassed detailed surveillance dossiers on virtually every internet user, and they've assigned each of us unique, persistent identifiers, like a Social Security Number for spying. These companies also allow advertisers – or anyone pretending to be an advertiser – to serve blobs of code (which is all an ad is) to anyone based on those identifiers.

This allowed an Israeli spyware company called Discover-Tech (which masquerades as an ad-tech company) to sell totalitarian governments and sleazy corporate mercenaries the ability to pluck individual internet users out of the billions who log in every day and then serve "malicious ads" (that is, blobs of arbitrary code) to those targeted users. These malicious ads contained "no-click, zero-day" attacks, which meant that they exploited previously unknown vulnerabilities to take over devices without any user interaction. The mere act of loading a web-page or opening an app that relied on one of these gigantic ad-tech companies to serve ads was enough to compromise your device. No clicks needed, and no warning.

Among the targets of this attack campaign were the computers of workers at Al Jazeera. They were attacked with malware from the mercenary spyware company Candiru (which now calls itself "Integrity Labs" because irony is not dead). blocks.text: A few months ago, I went to see Dr Hutchinson record his stand-up comedy special for the BBC - it's about his experiences working in the NHS as a Black doctor. As the title of the book implies, some of the public can be a mite suspicious that anyone with even a hint of melanin can rise beyond being a porter or, at a push, a nurse.

Much like Adam Kay's "This Is Going To Hurt", this is part biography, part rant about the NHS, and part humorous look at what it takes to be a modern doctor. Hutchinson's book has rather less gallows humour and rather more racism.

The problems of racial inequality in the NHS aren't just focussed on patients; they're also reflected in the way staff are treated. Rather than just recounting all the abuse he's been subject to, the book takes a good look at the actual statistics. Of course, this makes for slightly grim reading at times, so the frequent injections of humour are most welcome.
The UK quite often seems in the shadow of larger cultures. As the book points out:

This same issue is understudied in the UK – to the point where the absence of research is glaring. While we are clearly not just a little America, we aren’t so different that we can be confident we’re not replicating the same here.
Because of that, at times the book does feel a little bit like the "we have [racism] at home" meme.

There's an almost relentlessly cheery irreverence to some of the issues - but what else can you do? Sometimes it takes a good dose of comedy to cut through the bleakness. There's a slight streak of ageism within the book - especially when it comes to older doctors trying to use new technology. Although, to be fair, that was also my experience when working at NHSX. There are some people within the system who are desperate for it to remain preserved in aspic as even minor improvements are a threat to their position in the hierarchy.

A minor grumble, the problem I have with books like this - and with The Secret Barrister - is that a lot of the moaning about how hard it is to become a professional doctor / lawyer just generates a giant shrug from me. Every piece of medical media in the last 50 years talks about how bone-crunchingly hard it is. All I can think of is "none of this should be coming as a surprise to you!" Should it be easier (and less sleep depriving) to be a doctor? Sure! But given it isn't, perhaps dial down on the clichés of how uniquely awful your chosen career is.

The book isn't just a list of complaints, of course, everything is backed up with statistics (although unreferenced). Thankfully, the book ends with some practical suggestions of how the NHS can improve. It would certainly be interesting to read a version of this from 2046 to see how much has changed - given the improvements already bearing fruit, I'd hope that the UK health service would become much less racist over time.

blocks.text: NIST published a set of elliptic curves for cryptography in 2000. The seeds for the curves were supplied by the NSA, and cryptographers suspected the agency may have installed backdoors in the curves. And not without reason: the NSA did insert a backdoor in the Dual_EC_DRBG random number generator.
Two days ago researchers at Anthropic [1] showed that the NIST curves were not seeded with a backdoor. The rest of this post will give the background necessary to appreciate this result.

The security of elliptic curve cryptography depends on the difficult of solving the discrete logarithm problem. In the context of elliptic curve arithmetic, the analog of exponentiation is easy but the analog of taking logarithms is hard.

In general it’s not practical to compute discrete logarithms over large elliptic curves. But it could be easy for someone with inside information to compute discrete logarithms if something about the curve was not “general.”
Specifically, the NIST curves have the form
y² = x³ − 3x + b (mod p)

for various values of p [2], and the suspicion regards the choice of b. For nearly all values of b encryption over the elliptic curve should be secure, as far as we know, but in principle someone could engineer values of b to weaken the encryption.
So where did the b‘s come from? Were they chosen in good faith?

Concern over the choice of seeds, the b‘s, grew following the Snowden revelations. Daniel J. Bernstein emailed Jerry Solinas of the NSA on September 6, 2014 asking where the seeds had come from. Solinas replied in subsequent emails. He said the seeds were generated by hashing the ASCII representation of a humorous English message, but he could no longer remember the exact message or the precise hashing procedure.

On October 5, 2023 Philippo Valsorda announced a bounty for reverse engineering the origin of the NIST elliptic curve seeds. Two days ago researchers from Anthropic claimed the bounty. Valsorda verified the results and awarded the prize. It turns out Solinas found the curve seeds in good faith, but his memory had faded over the years since the curves were published. We now know he used a date, not a phrase, as part of the process of constructing the seeds.

The NIST curves have some nice properties, such as enabling some clever tricks for arithmetic in their base fields. But adoption of the curves has been held back over suspicion regarding their origin. Now the curves have been exhonorated. As Valdorda notes

… this nicely completes the “rehabilitation arc” of NIST elliptic curve cryptography, which I would now personally recommend over Curve25519/Ed25519/X25519. Just in time for them to be retired in favor of post-quantum signatures.

Some cleverness was required in order to come up with possibilities to check by brute force, but even that is sorta brute force at a higher level of abstraction. There has been speculation that labs are looking for weaknesses in cryptographic primitives and protocols, but that’s a different matter than searching for seeds.

[2] The curves P-192, P-224, P-256, P-384, and P-521 are built over the field of integers mod p, where the number of bits in p corresponds to the number in the name. The P-192 curve, for example, has as its base field the integers mod 2192 − 264 − 1, a 192-bit prime.

blocks.text: This week’s package management news, gathered from the package manager OPML feed collection, my posts and boosts on Mastodon, and anything people sent me.
Releases

pnpm 12.12 to 12.14 add a remoteCache setting that shares signed task results and dependency builds through a pnpr server or any server that implements the Turborepo Remote Cache API, and 12.14 adds sideEffectsCache.exclude for packages whose builds depend on system libraries outside the cache key. 12.13 adds pnpm profile and pnpm token, plus a storeIndexFormat: files setting that replaces the SQLite store index with one file per package for stores shared over a network filesystem.

mise 2026.10.8 to 2026.10.12 reads release lists, tags and attestations from its mise-versions host instead of api.github.com. A cold mise install of github: tools now makes no GitHub API requests, and mise ls-remote python went from 961 ms to 93 ms. 2026.10.9 fixes a trust bypass where an untrusted path: tool version could put a directory on PATH, and 2026.10.11 fixes a trust issue in remote task files.

vlt 1.4.0 turns the global store on by default on macOS, cloning packages with copy-on-write clonefile through node:ffi on Node 26.1 and later. A warm reinstall went from 9.6 s to 3.1 s. It also adds --save-types, which adds the matching @types package to devDependencies, and a vlt outdated command whose JSON output includes the install command for each update.

.NET 11 RC2 adds --min-publish-age-hours to dotnet nuget add source and dotnet nuget update source, which writes the minPublishAgeHours setting to nuget.config. According to the NuGet release notes, dotnet package add and dotnet package update apply the cooldown, and restoring a floating version fails with NU1020 when the cooldown excludes every matching version.

pixi 0.82.0 adds exclude-newer to the pixi global manifest, taking a date or a duration such as "7d", and accepts amdgpu = true or a specific GPU architecture such as "gfx90a" in platform declarations.
sbt 2.1.0-RC1 removes Apache Ivy from its dependencies and publishes without it. The metabuild moves to Scala 3.9, so plugins built for sbt 2.1 require sbt 2.1 or later.

pipx 1.18 runs upgrade-all, reinstall-all and install-all across several environments at once, and masks passwords in index and package URLs in its output and logs. 1.18.2 accepts absolute file URLs for local package installs.

uv 0.13.1 reports missing trusted hashes in resolution errors and adds preliminary parsing of PEP 825 variant labels in wheel filenames behind the wheel-variants preview. Tool and managed Python uninstalls now delete only their own storage directories and leave files next to them in place.

Spack Packages v2026.10.0 has 9,095 packages, up from 8,752 in 2026.06.0, and deprecates versions of several packages to address CVEs. It uses the v2.2 Package API, which works with Spack 1.0.0 and later. Its binaries are published to a releases/v2026.10 build cache mirror.

Renovate 44.161 to 44.165 resolves Go modules whose go-import meta tag names a mod proxy as of 44.164.0, which covers generated modules from a private Buf Schema Registry. An Ubuntu libcurl security update in the 44.161.0 base image made git send username-only credentials on the first request of a clone and omit them from the follow-up. Self-hosted users with a personal access token could no longer clone private repositories. The fix in 44.164.1 puts the token after x-access-token: in GitHub clone URLs. 44.164.9 adds a fallback username for SCM-Manager and is the version the maintainers recommend upgrading to. In the configuration JSON Schema, #46945 limits known object properties to their listed keys.

Dependabot Core 0.400.0 adds an apm (Agent Package Manager) ecosystem and supports Bun 1.4 lockfiles. zizmor 1.31 treats issue_comment as a dangerous trigger and flags cache-mode: write and write-only alongside dangerous triggers. typosquat-uses now also checks pre-commit inputs.
Also out:
Rust 1.99.1
conda 26.9.3
MacPorts 2.12.7
Helm 4.3.1
Helm 3.22.1
Podman 6.1.4
Podman 5.8.9
Terraform 1.17.0-rc2
Security

Package managers have an integrity problem (Keegan Ryan, Trail of Bits) runs 25 package managers with default settings against a simulated compromised repository behind mitmproxy. Go and vcpkg were the two that verified every download when there was no lockfile, and Go alone verified signatures by default. Fewer than half check lockfile hashes for tampering by default. The post proposes recording signer identity in lockfiles, backed by Sigstore identity signing and a transparency log.

rubygems.org now shows security warnings (Anton Bondaronok) on gem version pages, using OSV data refreshed every hour. Reports from the OpenSSF Malicious Packages project are labelled as malware, and older affected versions get a warning icon in the versions list. For now the warnings appear on rubygems.org pages only, and the next step is adding advisory data to the Compact Index so gem install and bundle install can show them. RubyGems 4.0.23 drops setuid, setgid and sticky bits from files when it extracts a gem.

PyPI now checks email reputation when an address is used to register or is added to an account, and rejects disposable addresses using a service donated by UserCheck. In the past month the check blocked 62 disposable domains and more than 120 disposable addresses on otherwise valid domains. PyPI banned outlook.com and hotmail.com in June 2024 after a malware campaign used them to register accounts in bulk, and with the check in place both domains are accepted again.

GitHub’s malware advisories now cover eight ecosystems (OpenSSF), up from npm only to npm, PyPI, Maven, RubyGems, NuGet, Go, crates.io and Composer. GitHub imports reports from the OpenSSF Malicious Packages repository, which contains more than 238,000 reports in OSV format, and Dependabot users with malware alerts turned on get the wider coverage with their existing configuration.

pnpm 12.12.1 and 11.28.6 make pnpm publish use an NPM_ID_TOKEN only when its aud claim matches the registry being published to, so a CI identity token goes only to the registry it was issued for. 12.12.0 makes an allowBuilds entry set to false take precedence over dangerouslyAllowAllBuilds, which previously ran those build scripts anyway.

Hex 2.5.3 fixes CVE-2026-96596, where a GNU sparse file in a package or docs tarball could put mix deps.get into an infinite loop. It also percent-encodes package names and versions in request URLs, so a /, ?, # or .. stays inside its path segment.

Docker Engine 29.9.1 updates containerd to 2.4.2 for three advisories where a malicious registry or crafted image could crash containerd or fill the host disk. OpenTofu 1.12.8 and Terraform 1.16.6 both fix excessive CPU usage when init connects to an attacker-controlled HTTP/2 server while installing dependencies, which Terraform’s notes track as CVE-2026-78669.

How the PHP Security Team Handles Your Reports (Alexandre Daubois, PHP Foundation) covers the triage process for php-src. Since 1 July the team has published 15 CVEs and closed 106 other reports as invalid, duplicates or not reproducible. Reports are reproduced on Linux, macOS and Windows under AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer. AI-written reports are accepted if the issue reproduces on a PHP build.
Articles

Nixpkgs for the frontend impaired (Farid Zakaria) introduces jinx, which compiles each .nix file to a TypeScript module. Across three platforms, 229,063 of nixpkgs’ 231,777 attributes produce the same drvPath as Nix, and the other 2,714 fail in both. It runs in Node 24 or a browser tab, three to five times slower than Nix. A second post, Always, sometimes, never, adds property checks such as single-writer and atomic-replace to Rewind VM’s schedule exploration.

Reproducible Builds in September 2026 covers the summit in Gothenburg and seven proposals for the SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH specification that are open for feedback until 1 December. dettrace now runs on most Debian and openSUSE architectures and supports PGO builds.

Thank you, Deno (Darcy Clarke, vlt), written after last week’s Cloudflare news, credits competition from Deno and Bun for features Node and npm later shipped, including fetch, the built-in test runner, type stripping and npm 12 making install scripts opt-in.
Elsewhere

Mend upgraded 184 open source organisations to the Renovate Community plan (Jamie Tanna, Mend). The upgrade covers about 3,000 repositories on Mend-hosted Renovate, including Argo, Biome, Nuxt, Tauri and the Rust project. The plan raises resource limits and concurrency and adds Merge Confidence. Other projects can request it in a Mend Hosted Request discussion.

VulnBump (Gabija Pasiunaite et al., arXiv) is a benchmark from Snyk of 307 dependency upgrade tasks covering 2,066 fixable vulnerabilities in 43 repositories across six package managers. A task passes when dependencies resolve and a rescan shows the fix, with the build and previously passing tests still green. Applying Snyk’s recommended version passed 46.9% of tasks, Claude Code on its own 59.6%, and Snyk’s remediation agent 90.2%.

Forgejo 17.0 reads FUNDING.yml to show a Donate button on repositories and profiles, and adds LFS views for locks and pointer files, plus a list of the commits that changed each file. The project recommends waiting before upgrading to 17.0.0 while it investigates an issue in that release that can stop pushes, merges and other code operations.

The Python Packaging Council has made its GitHub repository public, and will post the notes from each meeting there. People can file issues on the tracker to ask the council for a decision or for input.
git-pkgs

I tagged bibtex v0.1.0 (new), a Go library for reading BibTeX such as CITATION.bib files and entries embedded in READMEs, built for scanning untrusted input in bulk, alongside brief v0.14.2 and integrity v0.2.0.

blocks.text: Welcome to the reading list, a weekly roundup of news and links related to buildings, infrastructure, and industrial technology. This week we look at Icon’s fundraising, employment in China’s solar industry, grid-scale battery reliability, Tesla’s flying roadster, and more. Roughly 2/3rds of the reading list is paywalled, so for full access become a paid subscriber.
Housekeeping items this week:
I was on MTS Live talking about robots, prefabricated construction, and other things.
I’m quoted in this Dispatch article about data center construction.

From the annals of “suspicious discontinuities,” New York City has a tax break for new projects that set aside some proportion of the units as affordable housing called “485-x.” If a project has more than 99 units, the required share of units that are “affordable” goes up, and so do the wages that need to be paid for construction workers, resulting in a very large number of projects that are exactly 99 units. [X] [Housing Wire]

DR Horton, the largest homebuilder in the US, signed an agreement to access the services of Canadian construction automation startup Promise Robotics for more than 1250 homes. Promise seems to offer some sort of AI-driven, robotic factory-based construction service. “Promise Robotics applies AI across the homebuilding production process by interpreting existing home designs, generating production plans and robotic instructions, orchestrating manufacturing, and connecting that production with site installation.” [Promise Robotics] One possible future I see for construction automation is “AI + robotics changes the logic of prefab construction and makes it more attractive,” so it’ll be interesting to see if things like this play out.

Also in construction automation news, construction 3D printing startup Icon raises a $200 million series D, at a $1.4 billion valuation. [Dealroom] This is surprising to me: I had sort of assumed things weren’t going well for the company. Though this does seem to be a “down round” — in 2022 its valuation was supposedly “approaching $ 2 billion” — I’m nevertheless adjusting my probabilities of success for Icon upward somewhat.

Some interesting data from Harvard’s Joint Center for Housing Studies on immigrants in the US construction industry. One stat I found notable: between 2013 and 2024, the number of foreign-born workers who were construction laborers or carpenters increased massively, even as the number of native-born workers in those occupations declined. But for electricians and plumbers (licensed professions), most of the increase came from native-born workers. [Harvard JCHS]

GlobalFoundries, the semiconductor manufacturer that was spun off from AMD in 2009, will operate two new fabs planned for New York, funded by $21 billion from Japan. The US government is also taking a 4% equity stake in the company. [GlobalFoundries]
ASML says it can’t currently meet customer demand for lithography machines for 2027 and 2028, and is looking for ways to increase capacity. [ASML]
Ruthless competition in China’s solar industry: employment at China’s five biggest solar manufacturers fell 21% last year, and 31% the year before. [Reuters]

The US isn’t the only country with a small number of companies that make the grain-oriented electrical steel (GOES) needed for power transformers. Only two EU companies, Thyssenkrupp and Stalprodukt, make it, and as in the US they can’t make the highest quality steel. “The global leaders—the companies that make the world’s best GOES—by and large are in [South] Korea and Japan,” Alimento says. “In the U.S. and in the EU, domestic manufacturers are not capable of making that quality of GOES, because it is a heavily protected trade secret.” [IEEE Spectrum]
Thanks to ongoing memory shortages as a result of AI data center construction, smartphone shipments are down 20% year over year. [Counterpoint]

blocks.text: On October 17, 1985, Intel released its 386 CPU, also known as the 80386, and later, as the 386DX. The 386 changed the direction of the computer industry like no chip before it, and maybe since. The phrase “disruptive product” didn’t come into our lexicon until the mid 1990s, but when Harvard professor Clayton Christensen published his theory of disruptive innovation in 1995, the 386 powered one of his key examples.
IBM, the 386, and its repercussions

IBM was conflicted over the 386. Don Estridge, the engineer who oversaw the PC/AT, wanted to build a successor to the AT around the 386. He wanted to buy out Intel’s initial production run so that clonemakers wouldn’t be able to get adequate supplies of the chip. He’d done something similar in the 286 era.

The thing was, in the mid 1980s, IBM still had a very lucrative business selling minicomputers. These were medium-sized computers designed for applications where a mainframe would be overkill but a PC wasn’t powerful enough. In 1987, IBM sold $14 billion worth of minicomputers. IBM’s PC business was worth more like $4 billion a year in that era.

So there was a faction of IBM who didn’t want the 386 because it performed like a minicomputer. They didn’t want businesses buying a 386-based PC and loading Unix on it instead of buying a traditional minicomputer that cost twice as much.

The documentary Silicon Cowboys states that IBM wanted an exclusive on the 386 but doesn’t cite a source. Maybe the filmmaker misinterpreted what Don Estridge wanted to do, or maybe there was a third faction inside IBM with a slightly different opinion.
The IBM faction that didn’t want the 386 won out. And that caused two things to happen.
Intel shedding second sources

When IBM selected the Intel 8088 CPU to power its IBM PC 5150, IBM insisted on Intel licensing the design to at least one other chip manufacturer. This was to ensure that IBM would have a sufficient supply of chips to meet demand. It was also not a particularly unusual request. Both Apple and Atari had multiple sources for the chips they used in their computers, for instance.

Intel did IBM one better. Not only did they license the design to AMD, but they licensed it to several other companies as well. And after IBM selected the 80286 CPU to power its PC/AT, Intel amended the agreement with AMD and several others so they could manufacture not only 8088 and 8086 CPUs, but 80286 CPUs as well.
But with IBM uninterested in the 386, Intel had no reason to amend its agreement and extend the 386 to second sources. IBM wasn’t asking, and no one else had the clout to demand it.
AMD did clone the 386, but Intel fought it in court and kept it off the market until 1991, after the release of the 486.
Compaq taking the lead

Compaq famously released a 386-based PC in 1986, forcing IBM to do the same within 12 months. But that put IBM in catch-up mode, and of course, other 386 clones appeared in the meantime. The 386 was the first step in IBM losing control of the PC ecosystem it had built. The PS/2 line was the second. Compaq took the lead for a while, and by the mid 90s, we didn’t use the phrase “IBM compatible” so much anymore. Instead, “PC” took its place, or “Wintel,” an amalgamation of the words “Windows” and “Intel.”
And as Compaq faded, Intel and Microsoft increasingly took control over the direction of the ecosystem. IBM ultimately left the PC business in 2006.
Why the 386 was special

The 8088 was a bit of an oddball mashup 8-bit/16-bit CPU, designed to make porting 8-bit 8080 software easy, resulting in some design decisions that made lots of sense at the time but got in the way of future performance as time wore on. The 286 was more of a true 16-bit CPU and could be made to behave like it, or it could behave like a fast 8088 for compatibility reasons.

The 286 could run Unix, though it wasn’t the ideal Unix platform.
